title: Real Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP)
summary: Defines the Real Time Streaming Protocol, an application-level protocol for controlling the delivery of data with real-time properties such as audio and video. It acts like a remote control for streaming servers, supporting controlled, on-demand delivery. It was replaced by RFC 7826.

eli5.summary: A remote control for a streaming video server, with play, pause, and rewind buttons sent over the internet.

questions: how does real time streaming protocol work
subtitle: A network remote control for streaming servers: set up, play, pause and tear down audio and video streams.

tldr.problem: Audio and video streams need a standard way to be started, positioned, paused and stopped on a media server, separate from the way the media itself is carried.
tldr.mechanism: RTSP is an HTTP-like text protocol with methods such as DESCRIBE, SETUP, PLAY, PAUSE and TEARDOWN. The server keeps session state identified by a session ID, and the media usually flows over a different protocol such as RTP.
tldr.outcome: RTSP 1.0 is a Proposed Standard from April 1998. It was replaced by RFC 7826.

today: RFC 2326 defines RTSP 1.0 as a Proposed Standard from April 1998. It was obsoleted by RFC 7826, which is the one to read for the current specification.

sections.title: What RTSP Is For
sections.content:
The Real-Time Streaming Protocol establishes and controls one or several time-synchronized streams of continuous media such as audio and video. It does not typically deliver the streams itself. It acts as a "network remote control" for multimedia servers.

The protocol supports three operations: retrieving media from a media server, inviting a media server to a conference (to play media into it or record it), and adding media to an existing presentation, which is useful for live events. Requests can be handled by proxies, tunnels and caches as in HTTP/1.1.

The streams may use RTP, but RTSP does not depend on the transport used for the media. RFC 2326 does not define a format for the presentation description, which lists the streams being controlled; SDP is one such format.
sections.eli5: When you watch a video online, one part sends the pictures and another part is the remote. RTSP is only the remote: play, pause and stop.

sections.title: Sessions, State and HTTP Differences
sections.content:
RTSP is intentionally similar in syntax and operation to HTTP/1.1, so HTTP extension mechanisms can mostly be added to it. It differs in important ways. It has new methods and its own protocol identifier. A server needs to keep state by default, unlike stateless HTTP. Both client and server can issue requests. Media is carried out-of-band by a different protocol, with one exception. Text is UTF-8, and the Request-URI always holds the absolute URI.

There is no RTSP connection. Instead, a server keeps a session labeled by an identifier, and a session is not tied to a transport connection such as TCP. A client may open and close many connections during one session.

Five methods drive the state: SETUP allocates stream resources and starts a session, PLAY and RECORD start data flowing, PAUSE halts it without freeing resources, and TEARDOWN frees the resources and ends the session. The server generates session identifiers in response to SETUP, and the client must return it in every request for that session. The Session header can carry a timeout, which defaults to 60 seconds.
sections.eli5: Think of borrowing a video player at a library. SETUP is signing it out and getting a ticket number. PLAY and PAUSE use it, and TEARDOWN is handing it back.

sections.title: The RTSP Methods
sections.content:
A method name is case-sensitive. The methods are OPTIONS (required, no effect on state), DESCRIBE (recommended; fetches the presentation description, which is the media initialization step), ANNOUNCE (posts or updates a description), SETUP, PLAY, PAUSE, TEARDOWN, GET_PARAMETER, SET_PARAMETER, REDIRECT (the server tells the client to use another server) and RECORD. A server that lacks a method MUST answer 501 Not Implemented.

SETUP carries a Transport header with the client's acceptable transport parameters, and the response carries the ones the server chose. PLAY may include a Range header. PLAY requests are queued and executed in order, so a client can ask for seconds 10 to 15, then 20 to 25, then 30 to the end. After the range finishes, the stream pauses automatically.

PAUSE keeps server resources and the pause point, so a later PLAY with no Range resumes there. It discards queued PLAY requests. Time can be given as npt (normal play time), smpte or clock (UTC); a playback-only server MUST support npt.
sections.eli5: Each button on the remote has a name. PLAY starts, PAUSE holds your place, and TEARDOWN says you are done. You can even line up several PLAY requests like songs in a queue.

sections.title: Transport, Reliability and Interleaving
sections.content:
Systems implementing RTSP MUST support carrying it over TCP and MAY support UDP. The default port is 554 for both. The rtsp URL scheme assumes a persistent connection and rtspu means requests go without a connection. A client MAY pipeline requests, and the server MUST answer in the order received. Servers may also send requests to clients, but only on persistent connections.

Every request has a CSeq sequence number that grows by one for each distinct request. If a request is repeated because it was not acknowledged, it keeps its original number. Over a reliable transport such as TCP, requests MUST NOT be retransmitted by RTSP. Otherwise the sender may resend after a timeout of one round-trip time, with an initial round-trip estimate of 500 ms.

Where a firewall forces it, stream data such as RTP can be interleaved on the RTSP TCP connection. Each block starts with a dollar sign, a one-byte channel identifier and a two-byte length in network byte order, followed by exactly one packet. The RFC says interleaving should be avoided unless necessary, because it complicates clients and servers.
sections.eli5: The remote control normally talks to the video server on one wire while the video travels on another. If a strict gatekeeper only allows one wire, the video can be tucked inside the remote's wire in labelled packages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because RTSP is so close to HTTP, the HTTP/1.1 security considerations apply: authentication, protecting server logs, sensitive and personal information, attacks based on file and path names, Accept header privacy, DNS spoofing and Location header spoofing.

The RFC adds several RTSP-specific points. SETUP lets a client name a destination for the stream, which allows a remote-controlled denial-of-service attack, so a server SHOULD only allow client-specified destinations after verifying the client's identity, preferably with digest authentication or stronger. Because a session is not tied to a connection, a malicious client could guess session identifiers, so the server SHOULD use a large, random and non-sequential identifier. Servers SHOULD implement both basic and digest authentication, and the control stream may be encrypted. RTSP covers only stream control, so delivery protocols such as RTP carry their own security considerations.
sections.eli5: Since the remote can say where the video should be sent, a bad person could aim a flood of video at someone else. The server should check who you are first, and give out hard-to-guess ticket numbers.
